The relationship between vitamin D supplementation and regulatory T cells (Tregs) in apparently healthy individuals has been explored. Research suggests that vitamin D treatment may have an immunomodulatory effect, potentially increasing the percentage of Tregs, which are crucial for maintaining immune homeostasis.

This finding might help explain associations between vitamin D deficiency and autoimmune diseases, as it could contribute to the development or progression of these conditions. Current guidelines recommend treating vitamin D deficiency in patients with CKD (Chronic Kidney Disease) using ergocalciferol (vitamin D3), but suggest that higher or more frequent dosing may be beneficial for secondary hyperparathyroidism.

Regarding pediatric celiac disease, studies found no difference in 25(OH)D levels between children with and without CD (celiac disease). Additionally, a study suggested that vitamin D deficiency might be involved in the development of osteochondritis dissecans (OCD), a condition characterized by joint degeneration. Further research is needed to confirm these findings.

Vitamin C has been shown to reduce the prevalence of complex regional pain syndrome after wrist fractures and may also help prevent its development.

Research on immune suppression by lysosomotropic amines and cyclosporine suggests that combining these substances with chloroquine can lead to improved control of graft-versus-host disease (GVHD) in patients undergoing bone marrow transplants. However, the optimal time for acid suppression therapy is still being investigated.

Finally, studies on nucleos(t)ide analogs (NA) treatment for chronic hepatitis B suggest that stopping the medication may be possible in selected patients who meet certain criteria, such as not being cirrhotic, completed a minimum period of treatment, and have normal liver enzymes. However, more research is needed to determine the effectiveness of dexamethasone as an alternative to oral prednisone for pediatric asthma exacerbations.

In summary, vitamin D supplementation appears to be associated with increased regulatory T cell activity in apparently healthy individuals, which may contribute to autoimmune diseases. Further studies are necessary to fully understand its effects and potential benefits in various populations.
